Inherited from Old Armenian բան (ban). The main meaning of բան (ban) in Old Armenian was “word, speech, saying”. The sense “thing”, which is the only one surviving in modern Armenian, developed from the notion of speech → the subject of speech → the subject itself. Typologically compare Hebrew דבר (davar, “word, speech; thing”). For the “penis” sense development compare Azerbaijani şey and Turkish şey.

From the Old Armenian digraph ու (u) representing [u], composed of ո (o) + ւ (w). Some have contended that Old Armenian ու (u) was a diphthong, but this is incorrect: representing the monophthong [u] with a digraph is modelled on Ancient Greek ου (ou) pronounced as [u]. Compare likewise the digraphs Aghwan 𐕒𐕡 (u), Old Georgian ႭჃ (u), Old Church Slavonic оу (u).

Although attested only in modern texts, ատրճանակ (atrčanak) has a shape of classical Middle Iranian borrowings. Ačaṙean reconstructs the classical form as *ատրջանակ (*atrǰanak), supposedly borrowed from Middle Iranian *āturǰanak, composed of the words for ‘fire’ (see ատր- (atr-)) and ‘to hit, strike’ (see Proto-Indo-Iranian *ǰʰánti). For the suffix see -ակ (-ak). He speculates that the initial meaning was ‘device for making fire, fire-steel, flint’: compare Persian آتشزنه (âtaš-zana, “fire-steel, tinder-box”) from آتش زدن (âtaš zadan, “to set fire to”). From this meaning some modern author coined the sense ‘pistol’. For such a semantic development compare Turkish çakmaklı (“flintlock gun”) from çakmak (“fire-steel”). Compare also հրաճան (hračan), included in a couple of dictionaries as a translation of ‘musket’, which can be a learned Armenization of ատրճան (atrčan), by replacing Iranian *ātr- with native հուր (hur, “fire”).

Ačaṙean identifies with Old Armenian գլոր (glor, “rolling”). This is rejected by J̌ahukyan — because the dialectal forms point to Old Armenian *կլոր (*klor) with a կ- (k-) — who derives the word from Proto-Indo-European *gōl- (in case of կոլոր (kolor) from *gol-), from the root *gel- (“to press into a ball, be pressed into a ball; round”), + -որ (-or), whence e.g. Sanskrit गुल (gula, “any small globular substance”), ग्लौ (glau, “round lump”). See Pokorny for this root, without the Armenian. J̌ahukyan adduces also dialectal կլիկ (klik), կլոք (klokʻ), կղակ (kġak), կղան (kġan) as the reflexes of the same root.

The origin is uncertain. Ačaṙean derives from *պստ- (*pst-) + -իկ (-ik), comparing the first to Persian پست (past, “low; abject, ignoble”) as an Iranian borrowing. Earlier he also compared Chagatai پستك (pestek, “short, low”). Alternatively, perhaps derived from Proto-Indo-European *pstḗn (“breast”), by the sense development “suckling, nursling” → “small child” → “small”, either as an inheritance or a borrowing from the Iranian cognate: compare from that root Sanglechi štənōk (“new-born kid”) from *fštanya-ka-, Persian پستان (pestân, “breast”), and possibly Old Armenian սան (san, “nursling”). The same word is found in neighbouring languages: Persian لواش (lavâš), Talysh ləvoş, Georgian ლავაში (lavaši), Turkish lavaş, dialectal loş (Malatya), Azerbaijani lavaş, Turkmen lawaş, Tatar ләвәш (läwäş), Northern Kurdish lewaş, loş, lûşe, Central Kurdish لەواشە (lewaşe), Zazaki levaş, lewaş, lawaşe, lebaş, lebaşe, lebaşi, labaş, labaşe, lavaşi, all referring to types of flat bread. Some of these may be borrowed from Armenian. Lavash is usually considered an Armenian bread. Ačaṙean reports that in Tehran it is called نان ارمنی (nân-e armani, literally “Armenian bread”).
Almost certainly ultimately of Semitic origin: compare Samaritan Aramaic ࠋࠅࠔ (lwš /⁠lūš⁠/, “dough”), Aramaic לַיְשָׁא / לֵישָׁא (layšā, lēšā, “dough”), Classical Syriac ܠܝܫܐ (layšā, “lump of dough”), Akkadian 𒇷𒄿𒋙 (/⁠līšu⁠/, “dough, paste”), Biblical Hebrew לַיִשׁ (láyiš, “dough”), and particularly Assyrian Neo-Aramaic ܠܵܘܵܫܵܐ (lāwāšā, “a flap of thin bread”), Hulaulá lawaša (“long pitta bread”), Lishán Didán lawaša, lwaša (“flat thin cake of bread”), plausibly also Punic 𐤋𐤅𐤕 (lawāṯ (uncertain quantities), “Etruscan honeysuckle”) due to its wound petals, all from a verb Proto-Semitic *lawaṯ- (“to wind, to wallow”) which means in the Aramaic languages “to knead”.

Inherited from Middle Armenian գութան (gutʻan), also written as գուդան (gudan) and as գութա (gutʻa) in the phrase գութա մի (gutʻa mi, “one plough”). The latter should be understood as *գութան մի (*gutʻan mi) with the assimilation of ն (n) to մ (m) and the simplification of the double մմ (mm) to մ (m). Hence, the form *գութայ (*gutʻay) quoted by dictionaries based on that phrase is spurious.
A pan-Caucasian word of uncertain ultimate origin. Compare Georgian გუთანი (gutani), Mingrelian გუთანი (gutani); Ingush гота (gota), Chechen гота (gota); Dargwa гутан (gutan), Udi коьтаьн (kötän), Lezgi куьте́н (kütén), Avar кута́н (kután); Abkhaz а-куаҭана (a-kʼwatana), а-кәаҭа́н (a-kʷʼatán), Abaza кӏвата́н (kʷʼatán); Ossetian гу́тон (gúton), готон (goton); Northern Kurdish kotan; Azerbaijani kotan, Ottoman Turkish قوطان (kotan), dialectal Turkish köten, kötan, kotan, kutan, Karachay-Balkar гатон (gaton); Assyrian Neo-Aramaic ܟܘܬܢ (kûtân).
Abaev remarks that in all the languages the word refers to a heavy or improved version of the plough, whereas the regular plough is designated by a native word.
According to Genko (1930):
The question of the origin of such a widespread name of the plough seems to be insoluble by means of historical linguistics.

A dialectal term, unattested in Old or Middle Armenian. The earliest attestation is in Vilotte's Latin–Armenian dictionary of 1714. Recorded inter alia in the dialects of Yerevan, Tiflis and Karabakh, in the latter also as տա̈՛նդօ̈ռնը (tä́ndöṙnə), which may point to older *դանդուռն (*danduṙn). Ačaṙean compares with Mush dialect տանդռնիկ (tandṙnik, “a kind of wild edible green”) and Yerevan dialect դանդռի ծաղիկ (dandṙi caġik, “a kind of garden flower”). The plant name թանթռնիկ (tʻantʻṙnik) is probably the same word with the diminutive suffix -իկ (-ik), reflecting a Western dialect pronunciation.
The origin is unknown. Obviously connected with synonymous Georgian დანდური (danduri), Ingiloy dialect დანდრანუკა (dandranuḳa), Udi тӏаьнтӏоьр (ṭänṭör), the latter probably borrowed from the Karabakh dialect. Compare further Pashto تندولی (tandólaj, “purslane”).

Also from Kurdish: Hulaulá taši (“hand-spindle”), Chaldean Neo-Aramaic ܬܲܫܝܼܵܐ (taššiya, “spindle”), Lishán Didán taši, tašši (“distaff”). Dialectal Turkish terşi, teşi, teşik, tişe (“apparatus for skeining wool”), dialectal Azerbaijani teşi (“spindle”) are usually considered Armenian borrowings. The Kurdish too is often treated as an Armenian loan, but the opposite direction of borrowing is more likely because թեշի(կ) (tʻeši(k)) is not attested in Old or Middle Armenian and is limited to a few dialects, while the Kurdish is present in Central and Southern varieties and has a plausible native etymology (see below).
Ultimately probably from Proto-Iranian *častra- (“spindle”), whence also Munji čašīkȧ, čéša, Yidgha [script needed] (čɛšo), Pashto څاښی (śāẍay), څاشی (śāšay), Yaghnobi ташк (tašk), Ormuri [script needed] (tisk, “spindle”), Shahrudi taši, teši (“twister, spindle”). Note that the *č- → t- dissimilation is regular in Kurdish.

He also adduces the Semitic cognates of the Coptic word: Akkadian 𒉺𒅁𒁉𒂅 (/⁠šabbiṭu⁠/, “staff, sceptre”), Classical Syriac ܫܒܛܐ (šaḇṭā), Hebrew שֵׁבֶט (šḗḇeṭ, “rod, staff”). Modern scholarship derives the Coptic/Egyptian from Semitic. Compare also Siirt North Mesopotamian Arabic [script needed] (šabod).
Similar words are found in Iranian: compare Persian چفت (čaft).

However, the word is in fact recorded in Istanbul, Diyarbakır, Sivas, Palu and Çarsancak. Note also Süveydiye dialect սմպըկ (smpək), սմբըկ (smbək) referring to a kind of edible greens equivalent to Turkish almacık dikeni.
The origin is unknown.
Ačaṙyan derives from Arabic أَنَب (anab, “eggplant”) + -ուկ (-uk), via a form *ամբուկ (*ambuk), wherein ա (a) was then confused with similar-looking ս (s). But because the word is dialectal, such a literary confusion is unlikely.
Perhaps from an assumed root *սում(բ)- (*sum(b)-, “smooth; shaven”) or the like + -ուկ (-uk), thus “the smooth one”, referring to the smooth, glossy surface of the eggplant fruit, which root may also be contained in dialectal սմբուլ (smbul, “polished, smooth”), սմպատ (smpat, “having a smooth head”), սմպըլիկ (smpəlik, “having a shaven head”), սմբըլիկ (smbəlik, “leafless”), սնուկ (snuk, “very smooth”), սըն-եցնել (sən-ecʻnel, “to smooth, polish”) and the uncertain given name Սմպուկս (Smpuks). The -բ- (-b-) after -մ- (-m-) may be epenthetic in dialects: compare the examples given in Martirosyan 2010. This assumed root may be borrowed from Iranian, ultimately from Proto-Iranian *saH- (“to whet, cut”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱeh₃- (“to sharpen”), whence Baluchi سای- (sāy-, “to shave”), Central Kurdish سوون (sûn, “to whet, sharpen”), Gazi [script needed] (sǖn-, “to rub, shave off”), Persian ساد (sâd, “smooth, plane”), Sarikoli suδγ (“flat, smooth (surface)”), Persian سان (sân, “whetstone”), Central Kurdish ھەسان (hesan, “whetstone”), and according to Horn also Classical Persian سنباده (sumbāde, “whetstone”), to which the Iranian borrowing սմպատակ (smpatak, “touchstone”) is related (J̌ahukyan considers -ատակ (-atak) in the latter an Iranian suffix, as in յիշատակ (yišatak)). For the Iranian root see Cheung, without the Armenian. Compare also Zazaki sımıltkun (“hairless, smooth”).

From Old Armenian անսովոր (ansovor), from ան- (an-, “un-”) + սովոր (sovor, “accustomed; usual”).
Inherited from Middle Armenian ճամփորդ (čampʻord), a development of Old Armenian ճանապարհորդ (čanaparhord). By surface analysis, ճամփա (čampʻa) + -որդ (-ord). Doublet of ճանապարհորդ (čanaparhord).
From ան- (an-) + աղարտել (aġartel). In Old Armenian անաղարտելի (anałarteli) is attested.
From գնդ(ակ) (gnd(ak)) + -ա- (-a-) + ցրել (cʻrel). Calque of Russian пулемёт (pulemjót).
From Old Armenian անկանոն (ankanon). Equivalent to ան- (an-) + կանոն (kanon).
From Old Armenian գնդապետ (gndapet), from գունդ (gund) + -ա- (-a-) + պետ (pet).
From Old Armenian ձայնորդ (jaynord). By surface analysis, ձայն (jayn, “voice”) + -որդ (-ord, “-er”).
From Old Armenian բացօթեայ (bacʻōtʻeay). Equivalent to բաց (bacʻ) + օթ (ōtʻ) + -յա (-ya).
From Old Armenian անշշուկ (anššuk). By surface analysis, ան- (an-) + շշուկ (ššuk).
Borrowed from Azerbaijani talançı. Equivalent to թալան (tʻalan) + -չի (-čʻi).
From ձրի (jri) + -ա- (-a-) + -կեր (-ker). Literally, “eating gratis”. Compare Persian مفت خوار (moft-xvâr), Russian дармое́д (darmojéd) for identical formations.
Learned borrowing from Middle Armenian աճպարար (ačparar), from Arabic عَجَب (ʕajab) + Old Armenian առնեմ (aṙnem). The Eastern Armenian form is a spelling pronunciation.
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian բանախօս (banaxōs). By surface analysis, բան (ban) + -ա- (-a-) + խոսել (xosel).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian անշունչ (anšunčʻ), from ան- (an-) + շունչ (šunčʻ).
From ենթա- (entʻa-) + սպա (spa). Calque of German Unteroffizier or French sous-officier.
From Old Armenian կռապաշտ (kṙapašt). By surface analysis, կուռք (kuṙkʻ) + -ա- (-a-) + պաշտել (paštel).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian անտեսեմ (antesem), from անտես (antes), from ան- (an-) + տեսանեմ (tesanem).
From Old Armenian աղաջուր (ałaǰur). By surface analysis, աղ (aġ) + -ա- (-a-) + ջուր (ǰur).
From տասն (tasn, “ten”) + երեք (erekʻ, “three”). Old Armenian used երեքտասան (erekʻtasan).
Compound of տասն (tasn, “ten”) + չորս (čʻors, “four”). Old Armenian used չորեքտասան (čʻorekʻtasan).
Compound of տասն (tasn, “ten”) + հինգ (hing, “five”). Old Armenian used հնգետասան (hngetasan).
From Old Armenian մականուն (makanun). By surface analysis, մակ- (mak-) + անուն (anun).
From ինքն (inkʻn) + -ա- (-a-) + թռչել (tʻṙčʻel). Calque of Russian самолёт (samoljót).
From մահիճ (mahič) + -ա- (-a-) + կալնել (kalnel). Formally identical with Old Armenian մահճակալ (mahčakal, “bedridden”).

From Old Armenian փիլիսոփայ (pʻilisopʻay), borrowed from Classical Syriac ܦܝܠܘܣܘܦܐ (pīlōsōp̄ā), from Aramaic פִּילוֹסוֹפָא (pīlōsōp̄ā), borrowed from Ancient Greek φιλόσοφος (philósophos), from φῐ́λος (phĭ́los, “loving”) + σοφός (sophós, “wise”).
From Old Armenian խնձորենի (xnjoreni). By surface analysis, խնձոր (xnjor) + -ենի (-eni)
From Old Armenian ասորերէն (asorerēn). Equivalent to ասորի (asori) + -երեն (-eren).
From ժանտ (žant) + աքիս (akʻis). A learned 19th century creation.
From փոշի (pʻoši) + -ա- (-a-) + ծծել (ccel) + -իչ (-ičʻ). Calque of Russian пылесо́с (pylesós).
From կենս- (kens-) + -ա- (-a-) + -բան (-ban). Calque of French biologue.
From Middle Armenian սալորենի (saloreni). By surface analysis, սալոր (salor) + -ենի (-eni).
From ծով (cov) + -ա- (-a-) + ցուլ (cʻul). See also Old Armenian ծովացուլ (covacʻul).
From ամառ (amaṙ) + -անոց (-anocʻ). Old Armenian had ամարանոց (amaranocʻ).
Univerbation of ազգ (azg) + ու (u) + տակ (tak), literally “tribe and bottom”.
From աբեղ- (abeġ-, “abegha”) + -ա- (-a-) + ձագ (jag), because of the similarity of the crest with the veghar worn by an abegha.
From Old Armenian թմբկահար (tʻmbkahar). By surface analysis, թմբուկ (tʻmbuk) + -ա- (-a-) + հարել (harel).
From սառույց (saṙuycʻ) + -ա- (-a-) + հատել (hatel). Calque of Russian ледоре́з (ledoréz).
From Old Armenian համանուն (hamanun). Equivalent to համ- (ham-) + անուն (anun).
From Old Armenian ճանաչումն (čanačʻumn). Equivalent to ճանաչել (čanačʻel) + -ում (-um).
From Old Armenian անշրջելի (anšrǰeli). Equivalent to ան- (an-) + շրջելի (šrǰeli).
From Old Armenian արիւնոտ (ariwnot). Equivalent to արյուն (aryun) + -ոտ (-ot).
From Old Armenian ժայթքումն (žaytʻkʻumn). Equivalent to ժայթքել (žaytʻkʻel) + -ում (-um).
From Middle Armenian ափսոսանք (apʻsosankʻ). By surface analysis, ափսոսալ (apʻsosal) + -անք (-ankʻ).

From ծփալ (cpʻal, “to flutter”) + -ի (-i, botanical suffix). Calque of German Flatterulme, from flattern (“to flutter”). Probably coined by the Mekhitarists of Vienna, first appearing in Mēnēvišean's botany and hence copied into dictionaries.
From Old Armenian աղօթարար (ałōtʻarar). By surface analysis, աղոթել (aġotʻel) + -արար (-arar).
From ածուխ (acux) + -ա- (-a-) + ջուր (ǰur). Calque of Russian углево́д (uglevód).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian դիմադրեմ (dimadrem). By surface analysis, դեմ (dem) + -ա- (-a-) + դնել (dnel); compare French faire face, tenir tête.
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian միջավայր (miǰavayr), from մէջ (mēǰ) + -ա- (-a-) + վայր (vayr).
Semi-learned borrowing from Old Armenian պաշարումն (pašarumn). By surface analysis, պաշարել (pašarel) + -ում (-um).
From ական (akan) + -ա- (-a-) + նետել (netel). Calque of Russian миномёт (minomjót).
From Old Armenian բարեբախտ (barebaxt). By surface analysis, բարի (bari) + -ա- (-a-) + բախտ (baxt)
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian արագախօս (aragaxōs). By surface analysis, արագ (arag) + -ա- (-a-) + խոսել (xosel).

“Adam's fig”, from Ադամ (Adam) + -ա- (-a-) + թուզ (tʻuz). Compare English fig-banana (“a small variety of the banana”), French figuier d'Adam (name given to various varieties of bananas), Classical Persian انجیر آدم (anjīr-i ādam, “a kind of Indian fruit”, literally “Adam's fig”). Probably a modern literary creation.
From Old Armenian գերմանացի (germanacʻi). By surface analysis, Գերմանիա (Germania) + -ցի (-cʻi).
From կուրծք (kurckʻ) + -ա- (-a-) + նշան (nšan). Probably a calque of Russian нагру́дный знак (nagrúdnyj znak).
From բադ (bad, “duck”) + -ա- (-a-) + կտուց (ktucʻ, “bill”). Probably a calque of English duckbill.

From դաշն (dašn, “gentle, soft”) + ամուր (amur, “strong”). Calque of Italian pianoforte, composed of piano (“soft”) + forte (“loud, strong”) (so called because of the ability to vary the tone of the piano, as opposed to harpsichord).
From գետին (getin, “earth”) + -ա- (-a-) + նուշ (nuš, “almond”). Calque of Russian земляно́й оре́х (zemljanój oréx).
From Old Armenian եռանկիւն (eṙankiwn). By surface analysis, եր- (er-) + անկյուն (ankyun).
From նուշ (nuš, “almond”) + -իկ (-ik, “diminutive suffix”); because of the shape.

B2.etymology_text: From երկաթ (erkatʻ) + ուղի (uġi). Probably a calque of French chemin de fer.
From the root հանց- (hancʻ-), representing Old Armenian յանց (yancʻ), and -ա- (-a-) + գործել (gorcel).
From Old Armenian *մուլ- (*mul-, “to grind; to rub”) + -ակ (-ak).
From լույս (luys) + -ա- (-a-) + նկար (nkar). Calque of English photograph.
From Old Armenian հաստատուն (hastatun). By surface analysis, հաստատել (hastatel) + -ուն (-un).
From պահանջ (pahanǰ) + արկանել (arkanel). Modelled on առաջարկ (aṙaǰark).
From մեղր (meġr) + -ա- (-a-) + գինի (gini). Compare Old Armenian մեղրօղի (mełrōłi).
From ենթա- (entʻa-) + կայան (kayan). Calque of Russian подста́нция (podstáncija).
From Middle Armenian ջրաղացպան (ǰraġacʻpan). Equivalent to ջրաղաց (ǰraġacʻ) + -պան (-pan).
From Old Armenian սակաւախօս (sakawaxōs). By surface analysis, սակավ (sakav) + -ա- (-a-) + խոսել (xosel).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian բանադրանք (banadrankʻ), from բանադրեմ (banadrem) + -անք (-ankʻ).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian խաղաղարար (xałałarar). By surface analysis, խաղաղ (xaġaġ) + -արար (-arar).
From դեր (der) + -ա- (-a-) + կատարել (katarel). Calque of Russian исполни́тель ро́ли (ispolnítelʹ róli).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian արժանանամ (aržananam), from արժան (aržan) + -ան- (-an-).
From Old Armenian աղքատանոց (ałkʻatanocʻ). By surface analysis, աղքատ (aġkʻat) + -անոց (-anocʻ).
From ավտո- (avto-) + մեքենա (mekʻena). Calque of Russian автомаши́на (avtomašína).
From համակարգել (hamakargel, “to systematize”) + -իչ (-ičʻ, “-er”). Calque of French ordinateur.
Inherited from Old Armenian կոճակ (kočak), from կոճ- (koč-) + -ակ (-ak).
From կատու (katu, “cat”) + առյուծ (aṙyuc, “lion”). Coined in the 19th century.
From ծաղիկ (caġik, “flower”) + -ե- (-e-) + փունջ (pʻunǰ, “bunch”) or ծաղկյա (caġkya) + փունջ (pʻunǰ).
From մանր (manr, “small”) + է (ē, “being, object”), the root of էակ (ēak).
From մկն- (mkn-, “mouse”) + -իկ (-ik, “diminutive suffix”). The computing sense is a semantic loan from Russian мы́шка (mýška).
Inherited from Old Armenian պատան (patan), պատանք pl (patankʻ), from պատեմ (patem, “to wrap”) + -ան (-an).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian մական (makan).
From Old Armenian արքայասպան (arkʻayaspan). Equivalent to արքա (arkʻa) + -ա- (-a-) + սպանել (spanel).
From Old Armenian բազմագոյն (bazmagoyn). Equivalent to բազում (bazum) + -ա- (-a-) + գույն (guyn).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian անտեսանելի (antesaneli), from ան- (an-) + տեսանելի (tesaneli).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian աննշմարելի (annšmareli), from ան- (an-) + նշմարել (nšmarel) + -ի (-i).
From մանուկ (manuk) + -ա- (-a-) + պարտեզ (partez). Calque of German Kindergarten.
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian նաւահանգիստ (nawahangist), from նաւ (naw) + -ա- (-a-) + հանգիստ (hangist).

Unattested in Old or Middle Armenian. Found only in North-Western and North-Eastern dialects. Formed with the botanical suffix + -ենի (-eni).
Probably a Northeast Caucasian borrowing: compare Avar лъор (lˢor, “linden; hornbeam; aspen”), Andi лъор (lˢor, “elm; hornbeam; aspen”). According to Xajdakov, these are cognate with Lak хьхьири (x̂:iri), Dargwa хур (ꭓur), Tabasaran хяржж (ꭓjaržž), Godoberi хари (χari), all meaning “linden”. See also Nikolayev / Starostin for the Caucasian words.
From վրա (vra, “on”) + երթ (ertʻ, “driving”). Calque of Russian наезд (najezd).
From տժվժալ (tžvžal) + -իկ (-ik), probably because of the sound of frying.
From գիր (gir) + առնել (aṙnel). Compare գրի առնել (gri aṙnel).
From Middle Armenian մատղաշ (matġaš), from Old Armenian *մատղաշ (*matłaš), from *մաղտ- (*małt-), from Proto-Indo-European *ml̥d-, + -աշ (-aš). Compare մատաղ (matał).
From սխրանալ (sxranal, “to admire, to marvel at”) + -անք (-ankʻ).
From Old Armenian ստախօս (staxōs), from սուտ (sut) + -ա- (-a-) + խօսիմ (xōsim).
Sound-symbolic թմբլ- (tʻmbl-) + -իկ (-ik). Compare Turkish tombul (“fat”), Ossetian тымбыл (tymbyl, “round”), Persian تنبل (tanbal, “lazy”).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian ծրագիր (cragir). By surface analysis, ծիր (cir) + -ա- (-a-) + գիր (gir).
From Old Armenian վնասեմ (vnasem). By surface analysis, վնաս (vnas) + -ել (-el).
Inherited from Middle Armenian սրտանց (srtancʻ), սրտաց (srtacʻ), from սիրտ (sirt, “heart”). By surface analysis, սիրտ (sirt) + -անց (-ancʻ).
A literary formation from գլել (glel) + -ա- (-a-) + քար (kʻar). Probably a calque of Russian валу́н (valún).
From ջուր (ǰur, “water”) + շուն (šun, “dog”). For the semantics see կուղբ (kułb).
From Middle Armenian Նուբար (Nubar), from Persian نوبر (nowbar, “first fruits”), from نو (now, “new”) + بر (bar, “fruit”).
Inherited from Old Armenian հաճարի (hačari). According to Martirosyan, the dialectal form հաճարկի (hačarki) is probably from the diminutive հաճարուկ (hačaruk) + -ի (-i).
From գաղափար (gaġapʻar) + -ա- (-a-) + խոսել (xosel). Calque of French idéologue.
From տուն (tun) + փեսա (pʻesa). Possibly a calque of Classical Persian خَانَه دَامَاد (xāna dāmād).
From Old Armenian զիջումն (ziǰumn). Equivalent to զիջել (ziǰel) + -ում (-um).
From Old Armenian բացայայտումն (bacʻayaytumn). Equivalent to բացահայտել (bacʻahaytel) + -ում (-um).
From Old Armenian այդպէս (aydpēs). By surface analysis, այդ (ayd) + պես (pes).
From Old Armenian վերականգնեմ (verakangnem). Equivalent to վերա- (vera-) + կանգնել (kangnel).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian վերանորոգեմ (veranorogem). By surface analysis, վերա- (vera-) + նորոգել (norogel).
From Old Armenian զղջումն (złǰumn). Equivalent to զղջալ (zġǰal) + -ում (-um).
From հուր (hur) + -ա- (-a-) + -զեն (-zen). Formally identical with Old Armenian հրազէն (hrazēn).
From փուշ (pʻuš) + -ա- (-a-) + լար (lar). Calque of Russian колю́чая про́волока (koljúčaja próvoloka).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian կրկնակ (krknak). By surface analysis, կրկին (krkin) + -ակ (-ak).
From քիթ (kʻitʻ) + -ա- (-a-) + խոտ (xot). Probably a calque of Ottoman Turkish بورون اوتی (burun otu).
Inherited from Old Armenian թաքուն (tʻakʻun), from թաքչիմ (tʻakʻčʻim) + -ուն (-un).
Inherited from Middle Armenian կերցաւ (kercʻaw). By surface analysis, կեր- (ker-, “to eat”) + ցավ (cʻav).
Semi-learned borrowing from Old Armenian ցասումն (cʻasumn), from ցասնում (cʻasnum) + -ումն (-umn). Doublet of սասում (sasum).
Semi-learned borrowing from Old Armenian վիժումն (vižumn). By surface analysis, վիժել (vižel) + -ում (-um).
From դնել (dnel) + -ույք (-uykʻ). Calque of Russian ста́вка (stávka).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian կնամոլ (knamol), from կին (kin) + -ա- (-a-) + մոլիմ (molim).
From Old Armenian ձիագող (jiagoł). By surface analysis, ձի (ji, “horse”) + -ա- (-a-) + գող (goġ, “thief”).

From հանուր (hanur, “universal, general”) + -ա- (-a-) + գիտեմ (gitem, “I know”) + -արան (-aran, “-arium”). The first attestation is from 1868. հանրագէտ (hanragēt), հանրագիտական (hanragitakan, “encyclopedic”) are from 1861.
From վախ (vax) + -են- (-en-). The Old Armenian form is վախեմ (vaxem).
From լող (loġ) + -ան- (-an-). The form influenced by լոգանալ (loganal).
From գես (ges, “hair”) + աստղ (astġ, “star”), referring to the tail of a comet.
From նուշ (nuš, “almond”) + -ա- (-a-) + գեղձ (geġj, “gland”); because of the shape.
From Old Armenian զբօսանք (zbōsankʻ). Equivalent to զբոսնել (zbosnel) + -անք (-ankʻ).
Literally “smile/laugh in the palate”, from քիմք (kʻimkʻ) + ծիծաղ (cicaġ).
From հոգ (hog) + -ա- (-a-) + տանել (tanel). Compare Old Armenian հոգատարութիւն (hogatarutʻiwn). A back-formation from the latter is also possible.
From հին (hin, “paleo-”) + է (ē, “onto-”) + -ա- (-a-) + -բան (-ban, “-logist”). Calque of French paléontologue.
From Middle Armenian մասրենի (masreni). By surface analysis, մասուր (masur) + -ենի (-eni).

From հոլովել (holovel, “to roll”) + -ակ (-ak).
The sense “video clip” is a semantic loan from Russian ро́лик (rólik).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian դասական (dasakan).
From Old Armenian խոտակեր (xotaker). By surface analysis, խոտ (xot, “grass”) + -ա- (-a-, linking vowel) + կեր- (ker-, “to eat”).
From լի (li) + արժեք (aržekʻ). Calque of Russian полноце́нный (polnocénnyj).
From պանիր (panir, “cheese”) + խոտ (xot, “grass”), probably because it was added to cheese. See also ժաժիկ (žažik).
From անդր- (andr-) + շիրիմ (širim) + -յան (-yan). Compare Russian загро́бный (zagróbnyj) for the formation.
A modern literary creation as մամուխ (mamux) + -ենի (-eni).
From Old Armenian դիւրին (diwrin). Equivalent to դյուր (dyur) + -ին (-in, “adjective forming suffix”).
From Old Armenian կառապան (kaṙapan), equivalent to կառք (kaṙkʻ) + -ապան (-apan).
From Old Armenian նաւապետ (nawapet). Equivalent to նավ (nav) + -ա- (-a-) + պետ (pet).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian նուաճումն (nuačumn). Equivalent to նվաճել (nvačel) + -ում (-um).
From Old Armenian ուղեկից (ułekicʻ), from ուղի (ułi) + -ա- (-a-) + կցեմ (kcʻem).
From ուղեղ (uġeġ, “brain”) + -իկ (-ik, “diminutive suffix”). Calque of Latin cerebellum.
From Old Armenian բարեբախտաբար (barebaxtabar). Equivalent to բարեբախտ (barebaxt) + -աբար (-abar).
From փուշ (pʻuš, “thorn”) + արմավ (armav, “palm”). Probably a calque of German Stechpalme, coined by the Mekhitarists of Vienna.
From Old Armenian չարաճճի (čʻaračči), from չար (čʻar) + -ա- (-a-) + ճճի (čči).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian կնատեաց (knateacʻ), from կին (kin) + ատեամ (ateam). By surface analysis, կին (kin) + ատել (atel).
From զորք (zorkʻ) + -ա- (-a-) + կոչ (kočʻ) or զորք (zorkʻ) + -ա- (-a-) + կոչել (kočʻel).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian հովանոց (hovanocʻ). By surface analysis, հով (hov) + -անոց (-anocʻ).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian բարեհամբոյր (barehamboyr), from բարի (bari) + -ա- (-a-) + համբոյր (hamboyr).
From զորք (zorkʻ) + -ա- (-a-) + մաս (mas). Calque of Russian во́инская часть (vóinskaja častʹ).
From Old Armenian հողաթափ (hołatʻapʻ). By surface analysis, հող (hoġ) + -ա- (-a-) + թափել (tʻapʻel).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian ոսկեպատ (oskepat). By surface analysis, ոսկի (oski) + -ա- (-a-) + պատել (patel).
Inherited from Old Armenian շատախօս (šataxōs). By surface analysis, շատ (šat) + -ա- (-a-) + խոսել (xosel).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian սփոփանք (spʻopʻankʻ). By surface analysis, սփոփել (spʻopʻel) + -անք (-ankʻ).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian համոզիչ (hamozičʻ). By surface analysis, համոզել (hamozel) + -իչ (-ičʻ).

Does not seem to be attested in Old or Middle Armenian. The earliest appearance is in the second volume of HHB (1769) as a Grabar gloss to Ashkharhabar շէհպօյ (šēhpōy). According to Ačaṙean, created by some modern author as Classical Persian شاهپری /شهبری /شهبوی (šāhparī, šahbarī, šahbōy, “ambergris”) + -ակ (-ak) and massaged to look like a classical word borrowed from Middle Iranian. Note that Ačaṙean mistakenly thought ambergris is a flower. More fitting in meaning are the synonymous Classical Persian شَببویْ (šab-bōy) cited by Norayr and Ottoman Turkish شهبوی (şehboy) cited by Ačaṙean, but the 18th-century authors must have retrogradely equated the Ashkharhabar lex with the wrong item found in Persian dictionaries, due to the unwarranted Turkish change of شَب (šab) to شَهْ (šah) in this flower name, as the second half of شَهْبَرِی (šahbarī), شَاهْپَرِی (šāhparī) could be believed identical to بویْ (bōy) in view of the latter’s cognate բոյր (boyr).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian անթարգմանելի (antʻargmaneli). By surface analysis, ան- (an-) + թարգմանելի (tʻargmaneli).
From քնար (kʻnar) + -ա- (-a-) + հավ (hav), because of the shape of its tail.
From Old Armenian Փայլածու (Pʻaylacu), from փայլ (pʻayl, “radiance, shine”) + ածեմ (acem, “to carry, bring”).
From քար (kʻar) + ածուխ (acux). Compare Russian каменный уголь (kamennyj ugolʹ).
From Սիբիր (Sibir, “Siberia”) + ախտ (axt, “disease”). Calque of Russian сибирская язва (sibirskaja jazva).
From տող (toġ) + -ա- (-a-) + դարձ (darj) or տող (toġ) + -ա- (-a-) + դառնալ (daṙnal).
From շուրջ (šurǰ) + պար (par). The formation must have existed already in Old Armenian, whence Old Georgian შუშპარი (šušṗari) was borrowed. Doublet of շուշպար (šušpar).
From մատն- (matn-, “finger”) + -ա- (-a-) + քաշել (kʻašel, “to draw, to pull”). Narrow furrows are made on the surface of the bread by fingers.
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian անձնաւոր (anjnawor).
From Old Armenian հոյ (hoy) + -ա- (-a-) + կերտել (kertel) on the model of հոյակապ (hoyakap).
From Old Armenian նորապսակ (norapsak); by surface analysis, նոր (nor) + -ա- (-a-) + պսակել (psakel).
From երկինք (erkinkʻ) + -ա- (-a-) + քերել (kʻerel). Calque of Russian небоскрёб (neboskrjób).
From Old Armenian արատաւոր (aratawor). See արատ (arat) and -ավոր (-avor).
From տեսնել (tesnel) + -ա- (-a-) + արժան (aržan). Compare German sehenswürdig for the formation.
From խոզան (xozan) + -ուկ (-uk). Calque of translingual Setaria.
From Old Armenian լուացարան (luacʻaran). Equivalent to լվանալ (lvanal) + -արան (-aran).
From Middle Armenian հացհամեմ (hacʻhamem). Equivalent to հաց (hacʻ) + համեմ (hamem).
From զրահ (zrah) + -ա- (-a-) + կրել (krel). The noun senses are a semantic loan from Russian бронено́сец (bronenósec).
From ինքն (inkʻn) + -ա- (-a-) + թափել (tʻapʻel). Calque of Russian самосва́л (samosvál).
From գառն- (gaṙn-, “lamb”) + անգղ (angġ, “vulture”). Calque of German Lämmergeier. Probably coined by the Mekhitarists of Vienna.
From Old Armenian նմանատիպ (nmanatip). Equivalent to նման (nman) + -ա- (-a-) + տիպ (tip).
From Old Armenian *սրբագրեմ (*srbagrem), from սուրբ (surb) + -ա- (-a-) + գրեմ (grem).
From սավառնել (savaṙnel) + -ակ (-ak). Coined by Yervant Srmakeshkhanlian.
From մուրտ (murt, “myrtle”) + -ա- (-a-) + վարդ (vard, “rose”). A modern scholarly creation.
From Old Armenian ի ներքս արկանեմ (i nerkʻs arkanem). By surface analysis, ներ- (ner-) + արկել (arkel).
Learned borrowing from Middle Armenian երեսպաշտ (erespašt). By surface analysis, երես (eres) + պաշտել (paštel).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian որդեգրեմ (ordegrem), from որդի (ordi) + -ա- (-a-) + գրեմ (grem).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian հարկատու (harkatu). By surface analysis, հարկ (hark) + -ա- (-a-) + տալ (tal).

From Middle Armenian Վարդիթեր (Varditʻer), from վարդ (vard) + թեր (tʻer), the second element being a dialectal form of թերթ (tʻertʻ). Thus, the name means “rose petal”. Popularized by the novel Sos and Varditer by Perch Proshyan.
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian քառակողմ (kʻaṙakołm). By surface analysis, քառա- (kʻaṙa-) + կողմ (koġm).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian ընչաքաղց (ənčʻakʻałcʻ), from ինչք (inčʻkʻ, “property”) + -ա- (-a-) + քաղցնում (kʻałcʻnum, “to hunger after”).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian խռովարար (xṙovarar). By surface analysis, խռով (xṙov) + -արար (-arar).
Semi-learned borrowing from Old Armenian թլփատումն (tʻlpʻatumn). By surface analysis, թլփատել (tʻlpʻatel) + -ում (-um)
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian կիսաձայն (kisajayn). By surface analysis, կես (kes) + -ա- (-a-) + ձայն (jayn).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian մսավաճառ (msavačaṙ). By surface analysis, միս (mis, “meat”) + -ա- (-a-) + վաճառել (vačaṙel, “to sell”).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian ինքնակամ (inkʻnakam), from ինքն (inkʻn) + -ա- (-a-) + կամք (kamkʻ).
Semi-learned borrowing from Old Armenian յաւելումն (yawelumn). By surface analysis, հավելել (havelel) + -ում (-um).
From Old Armenian փոքրանամ (pʻokʻranam), from փոքր (pʻokʻr) + -ան- (-an-).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian ազատախօս (azataxōs). By surface analysis, ազատ (azat) + -ա- (-a-) + խոսել (xosel).
From Old Armenian զառանցանք (zaṙancʻankʻ). Equivalent to զառանցել (zaṙancʻel) + -անք (-ankʻ).
From փայտ (pʻayt) + ածուխ (acux). Compare Russian древесный уголь (drevesnyj ugolʹ) for the formation.
From Old Armenian միասնաբար (miasnabar), from միասին (miasin, “together”) + -բար (-bar, “-ly”).
From Old Armenian աղանդաւոր (ałandawor); see it for more.
Univerbation of նիստ (nist) + ու (u) + կաց (kacʻ), literally “the way one sits and stands”.
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian անցողական (ancʻołakan).
From հյուր (hyur) + -ա- (-a-) + խաղ (xaġ). Probably a calque of Russian гастро́ль (gastrólʹ).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian ասպնջական (aspnǰakan).
From կրկին (krkin) + -ա- (-a-) + կզակ (kzak). Probably a calque of Russian двойно́й подборо́док (dvojnój podboródok).
From զրուցել (zrucʻel) + -արան (-aran). The sense “arbor, gazebo, pavilion” is a semantic loan from Russian бесе́дка (besédka).
From մանր (manr) + -ա- (-a-) + ձուկ (juk). Formally equivalent to Old Armenian մանրաձուկն (manrajukn).
Denominal verb of ցուցադիր (cʻucʻadir), from ցույց (cʻuycʻ) + -ա- (-a-) + դնել (dnel).
From Old Armenian կառուցումն (kaṙucʻumn). Equivalent to կառուցել (kaṙucʻel) + -ում (-um).
From աքլոր (akʻlor) + -ան- (-an-). Compare the parallel formations in Azerbaijani xoruzlanmaq, Ottoman Turkish خروسلانمق (horoslanmak).
The origin is unknown. Suffixed with + -ենի (-eni). Not attested in Old or Middle Armenian. Listed in dictionaries as a dialectal word, but the dialectal area is not specified.
From դափնի (dapʻni, “laruel”) + -ա- (-a-) + վարդ (vard, “rose”). A modern calque of French laurier-rose or Ancient Greek ῥοδοδάφνη (rhododáphnē).
From սավառնել (savaṙnel) + -որդ (-ord). Coined by Yervant Srmakeshkhanlian.
From մանուկ (manuk) + -ա- (-a-) + տուն (tun). Calque of Russian де́тский дом (détskij dom).
From զորակոչ (zorakočʻ) + -իկ (-ik). Calque of Russian призывни́к (prizyvník).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian մարդատեաց (mardateacʻ), from մարդ (mard) + ատեամ (ateam). By surface analysis, մարդ (mard) + ատել (atel).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian կիսաստուած (kisastuac). By surface analysis, կես (kes) + աստված (astvac).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian հարկապարտ (harkapart), from հարկ (hark) + -ա- (-a-) + պարտիմ (partim).
From ճոպան (čopan) + ուղի (uġi). Calque of Russian кана́тная доро́га (kanátnaja doróga).
Semi-learned borrowing from Old Armenian հաստատումն (hastatumn). By surface analysis, հաստատել (hastatel) + -ում (-um).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian մանկաբարձ (mankabarj), from մանուկ (manuk) + -ա- (-a-) + բառնամ (baṙnam).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian ընդելանիմ (əndelanim), from ընդ (ənd) + ելանեմ (elanem).

From թուր (tʻur, “sword”) + -ա- (-a-) + շուշան (šušan, “lily”). Calque of German Schwertlilie (“iris”). Coined by the Mekhitarists of Vienna. The first attestation is in Čamčean 1851, using թրաշուշան (tʻrašušan) together with the synonym լուրջ շուշան (lurǰ šušan) to translate German Iris (see the quotation). Elsewhere in the text Schwertlilie is translated with լուրջ շուշան (lurǰ šušan) alone. In a footnote to թրաշուշան (tʻrašušan) the translator glosses the newly coined term with French iris, glaïeul, Ottoman Turkish մավի զամպագ (mavi zambak), գուզգուն գըլըճը (kuzkun kılıcı). Likely due to the French gloss glaïeul which means gladiolus the meaning later shifted to this flower.

From լեռն- (leṙn-, “mountain”) + -ա- (-a-) + վարդ (vard, “rose”). A modern scholarly creation, coined by the Mekhitarists of Vienna. The first attestation is in Čamčean 1851, using Պոնտոսի լեռնավարդ (Pontosi leṙnavard) to translate Azalea pontica, syn. of Rhododendron luteum (see the quotation).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian պատկառուկ (patkaṙuk). By surface analysis, պատկառել (patkaṙel) + -ուկ (-uk). The flower name was probably coined by the Mekhitarists of Venice.
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian հիւրասէր (hiwrasēr). By surface analysis, հյուր (hyur) + -ա- (-a-) + սիրել (sirel).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian կասկածանք (kaskacankʻ). By surface analysis, կասկածել (kaskacel) + -անք (-ankʻ).
From Old Armenian տխրութիւն (txrutʻiwn); see it for more.
From Old Armenian անապատական (anapatakan); see below.
From Old Armenian փական (pʻakan); see it for more.
From Old Armenian ծերութիւն (cerutʻiwn); see it for more.
From Old Armenian գարնանային (garnanayin); see it for more.
A modern literary formation from մուշկ (mušk) + ընկույզ (ənkuyz).
Denominal verb of նկարահան (nkarahan), from նկար (nkar) + -ա- (-a-) + հանել (hanel).
From ծով (cov) + -ա- (-a-) + խոզուկ (xozuk). Calque of Russian морска́я сви́нка (morskája svínka).
From միջոց (miǰocʻ, “measure”) + առնել (aṙnel, “to take”) + -ում (-um). Probably a calque of Russian мероприя́тие (meroprijátije).
From կինո- (kino-) + թատրոն (tʻatron). Calque of Russian кинотеа́тр (kinoteátr).
From Old Armenian շրջափակումն (šrǰapʻakumn). Equivalent to շրջափակել (šrǰapʻakel) + -ում (-um).
From զրահ (zrah) + -ա- (-a-) + գնացք (gnacʻkʻ). Calque of Russian бронепо́езд (bronepójezd).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian մեղուաբոյծ (mełuaboyc), from մեղու (mełu) + -ա- (-a-) + բուծանեմ (bucanem).
From ներկայում (nerkayum, locative singular of ներկա (nerka)) + -ս (-s, demonstrative suffix).

Mkrtchyan considers this to be derived from չին աշխարհից (čʻin ašxarhicʻ, “from the Chinese world”), using immense distance as a way to describe something/someone as exotic. Ačaṙean disputes that and gives the explanation of ոչ (očʻ) + աշխարհ (ašxarh).
From խցան (xcʻan) + -ա- (-a-) + կաղնի (kaġni). Calque of Russian про́бковый дуб (próbkovyj dub).

From ինքն (inkʻn) + -ա- (-a-) + գլուխ (glux). Compare Turkish kendi başına. In the ecclesiastical sense a learned borrowing from Old Armenian ինքնագլուխ (inkʻnaglux) which is a calque of Ancient Greek αὐτοκέφαλος (autoképhalos).
From սպասարկել (spasarkel) + -ում (-um). Calque of Russian обслу́живание (obslúživanije).
From հողմ (hoġm, “wind”) + -ա- (-a-) + ծաղիկ (caġik, “flower”). Calque of Ancient Greek ἀνεμώνη (anemṓnē). Probably coined by the Mekhitarists of Venice.
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian բազմաստուած (bazmastuac). By surface analysis, բազում (bazum) + աստված (astvac).
From թավիշ (tʻaviš) + -ա- (-a-) + ծաղիկ (caġik). A purism created in the 19th century, probably a calque of Ottoman Turkish قطیفه چیچكی (kadife çiçeği).
Learned borrowing from Old Armenian ամբողջապէս (ambołǰapēs). By surface analysis, ամբողջ (amboġǰ) + -ապես (-apes).
From հանուր (hanur) + -ա- (-a-) + խանութ (xanutʻ). Calque of Russian универма́г (univermág), универса́льный магази́н (universálʹnyj magazín).
From տիեզերք (tiezerkʻ) + -ա- (-a-) + գնալ (gnal). Calque of Russian космо-навт (kosmo-navt). Formally identical with Old Armenian տիեզերագնաց (tiezeragnacʻ).
From Old Armenian հոյ (hoy) + -ա- (-a-) + կառուցել (kaṙucʻel) on the model of հոյակապ (hoyakap).
From շեֆ (šef) + խոհարար (xoharar). Calque of Russian шеф-по́вар (šef-póvar).
From ծուխ (cux) + -ա- (-a-) + ծածկույթ (cackuytʻ). Calque of Russian дымова́я заве́са (dymovája zavésa).
From կես (kes) + -ա- (-a-) + պաշտպան (paštpan). Calque of Russian полузащи́тник (poluzaščítnik).
From մանուկ (manuk) + -ա- (-a-) + սայլակ (saylak). Calque of Russian де́тская коля́ска (détskaja koljáska).
From կես (kes) + -ա- (-a-) + կայարան (kayaran). Calque of Russian полуста́нок (polustánok).

From մարմին (marmin, “body”) + -ա- (-a-) + վաճառել (vačaṙel, “to sell”). Compare Persian تنفروش (tan-foruš) for a similar formation; compare also English sell one's body, French vendre son corps. Formally identical with Old Armenian մարմնավաճառ (marmnavačaṙ, “meat seller”).
From հողմ (hoġm) + -ա- (-a-) + շարժիչ (šaržičʻ). Calque of Russian ветродви́гатель (vetrodvígatelʹ).
